title: Hodges's soprano tone versus Sidney Bechet's
summary: Hodges took his inspiration from Bechet, but Waters found Hodges's tone smoother and purer and Bechet's vibrato wide, while Bechet had the greater jazz licks.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: You already knew about Sidney Bechet?
In person or you only knew him through records, or don't you remember?
I don't know, but I think it was records.
And was he on a Bechet kick on soprano?

Well, n-, here's what he said to himself, 'I got my', got his inspiration from - I think I said that before - he got his inspiration from Sidney Bechet. But I thought that Johnny's tone was more cultivated than Sidney's. I thought that Sidney's vibrato was a little bit wide, shaky, wherein Johnny's was smooth. And that's the type of soprano I was playing also. But the ideas that he had, you could detect Sidney, you see? Certain things in his choruses, you know. Perfect. What I'm gettin' at, what I really gettin' at, I mean for the tone quality, not the musicianship, not the jazz licks, 'cause Sidney was something else for that, he was something else, I mean. He had real licks for jazz, you know - I heard Louie and him record, it's a record that he made for Louie, that five, that five, what's it called that, Louie Armstrong Five or something -
Hot Five. He made a record with that group and you can't tell who's better.
Oh, you mean Clarence Williams's Blue Five?
Yeah, may, could be. I mean with Louie Armstrong and (PS joins on 'and') -
